channel.title: The MisterLibrarian Bible Project
channel.description: A fresh translation of the Bible into modern English, made from the original Hebrew and Greek one chapter at a time.

item.title: Mark 13
item.description: Leaving the temple courts for good, a disciple admires “what massive stones, what massive buildings” — and gets back the prediction Mark 12's own closing note already promised: not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives, opposite the temple, four disciples…

item.title: Mark 12
item.description: A parable told against the chief priests who just failed to answer a question of their own: a vineyard, an absentee owner, three waves of beaten servants, and a beloved son the tenants kill and cast out of the vineyard — Matthew's parallel reverses the order, casting him out…

item.title: Mark 11
item.description: The road finally reaches Jerusalem. Two disciples fetch a colt “on which no one has ever yet sat” from a village whose own name is Aramaic for “house of unripe figs” — and Mark's crowd, unlike Matthew's, blesses “the coming kingdom of our father David” rather than calling…

item.title: Mark 10
item.description: Pharisees test Jesus on divorce, and the answer reaches past Moses' permission — NOT a command, a distinction Matthew already made of this same question — to Genesis itself: 'from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female.' Little children are brought to be…

item.title: Mark 9
item.description: Six days later, three disciples on a high mountain, and Jesus is TRANSFIGURED — the same verb Matthew keeps and Luke throws away for a plainer 'his face became different.' Elijah appears “with” Moses — Mark's own word order, reversed from Matthew's — and a voice from a cloud…

item.title: Mark 8
item.description: A second miraculous feeding, and the chapter turns on the fact that Mark tells it with different words: the twelve baskets of the five thousand are kophinoi, a Jewish traveller's small hand-basket, and the seven here are spyrides, a hamper big enough to lower a grown man over…

item.title: Acts 15
item.description: The first council the church ever holds, called to decide whether a Gentile has to become a Jew first — and the letter it sends still carries, almost as an afterthought beside the free pass on the law of Moses, the ancient command to abstain from blood (Genesis 9:4, Leviticus…

item.title: Revelation 13
item.description: A beast rises out of the sea -- ten horns, seven heads, the dragon's own body from the chapter before, and now a composite of every animal Daniel's four-beast vision needed a separate scene to describe: a leopard's body, a bear's feet, a lion's mouth. One of its heads bears a…

item.title: Numbers 36
item.description: The last chapter of Numbers, and it is an appeal against a ruling the book already made. In Numbers 27 the daughters of Zelophehad won their dead father’s land; here the men of their own clan draw near — the same verb the sisters used, in the masculine — and point out that if…

item.title: Numbers 35
item.description: The cities of refuge — and the chapter is where the sixth commandment’s own verb lives: ratzach, the word in lo tirtzach, stands here twenty times out of forty-five in the whole Hebrew Bible, in fourteen of thirty-four verses. ⭐ Hebrew uses ONE word for the man who kills by…

item.title: Numbers 34
item.description: The borders of Canaan, drawn corner to corner — and the chapter is a DEED, not a description: gvul, border, stands in it sixteen times in twenty-nine verses, more than in any other chapter of the Torah and nearly three times the runner-up. ⭐ The land is not GIVEN here, it…

item.title: Numbers 33
item.description: Moses writes the whole forty-year itinerary himself, stage by stage, forty-two camps from Rameses to the plains of Moab, and its opening line collects a promise made forty years earlier: Exodus 12:12 has Jehovah say he WILL execute judgments on Egypt's gods; here, in the…

item.title: Numbers 32
item.description: Reuben and Gad, rich in cattle, ask to settle east of the Jordan instead of crossing into Canaan — and Moses answers not with a ruling but with a history lesson, retelling Numbers 13-14 almost word for word to men who were children when the scouts' report cost their parents…

item.title: Numbers 31
item.description: Moses sends an army to avenge Israel on Midian, and the campaign that follows refuses to stay simple. Every fighting man is killed and every city burned — and Balaam, the gentile seer who filled three earlier chapters with his own voice, dies in six words, the same clause as…

item.title: Numbers 30
item.description: A single law of vows, and the shelf cannot even agree where it begins — only Douay-Rheims and Geneva 1599 side with the Masoretic text in opening the chapter with the sentence Numbers 29's own closing note promised; the other eleven witnesses on this project's shelf attach it…

item.title: Numbers 29
item.description: Jehovah completes the offering calendar Numbers 28 began, and this half is where the chapter starts naming its own seams instead of leaving them silent. ⭐ The New Year's day of blowing (v1) is never called a new year here or in its parallel at Leviticus 23 — Exodus 12:2…

item.title: Numbers 28
item.description: Jehovah hands Moses the tabernacle's fixed offering calendar, and the chapter's whole grammar is one word: tamid, continual — every occasion from here on is layered ON the twice-daily lamb, never instead of it. ⭐ The numbers agree exactly with Exodus 29:38-42, unchanged…

item.title: Numbers 27
item.description: Five women walk to the front of the camp and change a law. ⭐ Zelophehad’s daughters — named in a census two chapters ago for no stated reason — stand before Moses, the priest, the chieftains and the whole congregation and argue a case: our father was not in Korah’s faction…

item.title: Numbers 26
item.description: The book counts its people a second time, and the arithmetic is the argument. ⚠ Numbers 1 counted a generation at Sinai; this counts their children on the plains of Moab, thirty-eight years later, in the same words — and the last three verses explain why: not one man of the…

item.title: Numbers 25
item.description: The disaster Balaam could not deliver, arriving without him. ⚠ Israel camps at Shittim — the place named after ACACIAS, the wood its own tabernacle is built from — and the people begin sleeping with Moabite women and eating at their gods’ sacrifices. ⭐ The verb for what…

item.title: Numbers 24
item.description: Balak has paid for a curse three times and is about to be told what will happen to him. ⚠ The chapter opens by reporting that Balaam stopped going toward omens — the plural of the very noun he had just denied of Israel in the previous chapter, so the man abandons his…

item.title: Numbers 23
item.description: Balak has hired a curse and he is going to be billed for two blessings. Seven altars go up, then seven more, then seven more — twenty-one bulls and twenty-one rams across three summits — and each time the answer comes back the wrong way round. ⚠ Read the narrator’s verb…

item.title: Numbers 22
item.description: Israel is camped on the plains of Moab and the story leaves them entirely for three chapters. Balak king of Moab has just watched what happened to Sihon and Og, works out that he cannot win a battle, and goes looking for a weapon an army cannot answer — so he sends four…

item.title: Numbers 21
item.description: The hinge of the book, and the chapter every Bible reader half-remembers. Israel destroys the Canaanite king of Arad and names the place Hormah — the same place the previous generation was beaten back to, now renamed by a victory instead of a defeat. Then the food and the…

item.title: Numbers 20
item.description: ⚠ Thirty-eight years pass in the white space before v1, and the chapter opens by burying Miriam in a single clause — no mourning recorded, where Aaron will get thirty days by v29. ⭐ Then something no translation can carry: at v10 Moses turns on the people and shouts ha-morim…

item.title: Numbers 19
item.description: ⚠ The chapter everyone knows as the RED HEIFER, which this translation calls a red COW — because parah means a cow, because Hebrew's actual word for a heifer (eglah) is already spent on Genesis 15:9, and because the shelf is not on the famous side: four say heifer (KJV, ASV…

item.title: Numbers 18
item.description: ⚠ The chapter is addressed to AARON, and that is the finding: searched across the whole Hebrew Bible, God speaks directly to Aaron with Moses not in the sentence in exactly five verses, and THREE of them are here (vv1, 8, 20). The other sustained one is Leviticus 10:8, the…

item.title: Numbers 17
item.description: ⚠ Read the versification note before anything else: the Hebrew chapter has 28 verses and holds TWO episodes, so vv1-15 here are printed in every English Bible as Numbers 16:36-50, and vv16-28 as Numbers 17:1-13. Nothing is added or missing on either side — the same text is…

item.title: Numbers 16
item.description: Korah's rebellion — and it opens on a broken sentence. ⚠ And Korah took, says the Hebrew, and never says what he took: the verb wants an object and there isn't one, and the seven versions checked here invent seven different solutions, from ‘took men’ to ‘became insolent’ to…

item.title: Numbers 15
item.description: A law about arriving, addressed to the generation that has just been told it will never arrive: the words immediately following the sentence in the wilderness are ‘when you come into the land.’ Grain and wine become a fixed accompaniment to every animal offering, on a sliding…
